questions.question_text: Does $W=\dfrac{20}{t}$ represent inverse variation? If so, state the constant of variation.

options.why: Confused $y=k/x$ with $y=kx$ and took the reciprocal of the numerator.
Mistook the inverse-variation form $y=k/x$ for the direct form $y=kx$.
Identified the variable $t$ itself as the constant of variation instead of the numerator.

questions.solution_text:
$W=\dfrac{20}{t}$ is in the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$, so this is inverse variation.
Constant of variation: $k=20$

options.text: No, because of the subtracted constant $3$

options.why: Ignored the subtracted constant term and read $k$ straight off the numerator.

options.text: No, because $x$ is in the denominator
options.why: Misidentified the required denominator form as the defect, when the real issue is the subtracted constant.
Combined $12$ and $3$ into a single constant instead of checking the form.

questions.solution_text:
$y=\dfrac{12}{x}-3$ has a constant term $3$ subtracted, so it is not in the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.
This is not inverse variation.

options.text: No, because $x$ is multiplied by a constant, not divided into one

options.why: Read off the coefficient of $x$ without checking whether $x$ is multiplied or divided.
Took the reciprocal of the coefficient, confusing the direct and inverse variation forms.

options.text: No, because $8$ is too large to be a constant of variation
options.why: Invented a size restriction on $k$ that doesn't exist — any nonzero value can be a constant of variation.

questions.solution_text:
$y=8x$ has $x$ multiplied by a constant, not divided into a constant, so it is not in the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.
This is not inverse variation.

options.text: No, because $x$ is raised to a power in the denominator

options.why: Read off the numerator without checking whether $x$ itself is only divided into the constant.
Squared the numerator instead of checking the power on $x$ in the denominator.

options.text: No, because $6$ is too small to be a constant of variation
options.why: Invented a restriction on the size of the numerator instead of checking the power on $x$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=\dfrac{6}{x^{2}}$ has $x$ raised to a power in the denominator, not simply divided into a constant, so it is not in the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.
This is not inverse variation.

questions.question_text: A fixed amount of prize money is shared equally among the winners of a competition. Is the amount each winner receives inversely proportional to the number of winners? Explain.

options.text: Yes, because doubling the number of winners halves the amount each one receives
No, because more winners means a bigger celebration
options.why: Introduced an irrelevant factor that has no bearing on the mathematical relationship.

options.text: No, because the total prize could change
options.why: Introduced a condition (a changing total) that isn't stated in the scenario.

options.text: Yes, because more winners always means less money each
options.why: Confirmed only that the share decreases with more winners, without checking it decreases by the same factor.

questions.solution_text:
Doubling the number of winners halves the amount each one receives, since the fixed prize pool is always divided evenly.
This is inverse variation.

questions.question_text: It takes $5$ painters $12$ hours to paint a house. The time $t$ varies inversely with the number of painters $p$. Find the constant of variation.

options.why: Divided $12$ by $5$ instead of multiplying to find $xy$.
Added the number of painters and the hours instead of multiplying.
Took the reciprocal of the correct product $xy$.

questions.question_text: $y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$, and $y=9$ when $x=4$. Find the constant of variation $k$.

options.why: Divided $x$ by $y$ instead of multiplying them to find $k$.
Added $y$ and $x$ together instead of multiplying.
Took the reciprocal of the correct product $xy$.

questions.question_text: $C$ is inversely proportional to $r$, and $C=-6$ when $r=4$. Omar says inverse variation constants must be positive. Is he correct? Find the constant of variation.

options.text: Yes, he's correct; this cannot be inverse variation
options.why: Wrongly assumed the constant of variation must be positive — a negative $k$ is still valid.
Dropped the negative sign when multiplying instead of keeping $C$ negative in the calculation.
Divided $C$ by $r$ instead of multiplying to find the constant of variation.

questions.solution_text:
Inverse variation only requires $Cr$ to be constant — the constant of variation can be negative.
$k=Cr$
$=-6 \times 4$
$=-24$
Omar is incorrect; this is inverse variation with constant of variation $k=-24$.
